metaTitle: Best Portable Air Conditioners for Rooms (2026)
metaDescription: Seven portable air conditioners compared on SACC cooling, dual or single hose design, noise, drainage and room size claims, from 8,000 to 14,000 BTU.
expertTake: The Whynter ARC-1230WN dual hose inverter unit is our top pick for its efficient dual hose design, auto drain and smart control. The HOMCOM 8,000 BTU is the value pick for a small, sealed room. Skip a portable unit if a window air conditioner fits your window, because it will cool the same room for less and with less noise.
introParagraphs: A portable air conditioner is a floor standing cooler that vents its hot air through a hose out of a window. It suits rooms where a window unit is not allowed or does not fit, such as a sliding window, a casement or a rental with strict rules. It costs more to run than a window unit of the same capacity, and it is louder.

The headline BTU number on the box is often not the real cooling figure, and the number of hoses changes how well a unit works. This guide compares seven portable units, explains the ratings and the hose design, and says where each one belongs in a living room.

products.name: Whynter ARC-1230WN 14,000 BTU Dual Hose Inverter Portable AC, Smart Wi-Fi

specList.label: Hoses
specList.value: Dual hose, separate intake and exhaust

specList.label: Features
specList.value: Wi-Fi app, built in dehumidifier with auto drain

products.description:
The Whynter ARC-1230WN is a dual hose unit with an inverter compressor, Wi-Fi app and voice control, and a built in dehumidifier with automatic drain. Dual hose means one hose brings outdoor air in to cool the condenser and a second sends the heat out, so the unit does not pull cooled room air out of the house. That is the main efficiency advantage over a single hose unit.

The inverter compressor varies its speed instead of cycling on and off, which usually means steadier temperatures and a quieter run. It costs close to the top of the group, and it is a heavy, large machine, so it will not suit a tiny room or a flat with stairs. Against the Midea Duo, which also uses a dual hose idea and sits at the top of the cost range, the Whynter is a more established design with an auto drain.

Installation is the main task. You need a window kit, short and straight hoses and a clear spot at least 12 inches from walls and curtains. Wash the filter every two weeks in use and check that the auto drain is clear.
products.bestFor: Living rooms and large bedrooms that need efficient cooling with no window unit.
pros: Dual hose design avoids pulling cooled room air out through the exhaust
Inverter compressor gives steadier temperature and quieter running
Built in dehumidifier with auto drain reduces emptying a bucket
Wi-Fi app and voice control allow scheduling from a phone
cons: High cost and a large, heavy body that is hard to move upstairs
Still audible in the room because the compressor sits inside

products.name: Midea Duo 14,000 BTU Portable Air Conditioner with Heat, Hose in Hose Inverter
products.description:
The Midea Duo uses a hose in hose design, in which a single thick hose carries the intake and exhaust air in separate channels. The listing states 14,000 BTU with a 12,000 BTU SACC rating, a variable speed inverter and a heating mode. That SACC number is high compared with the other 14,000 BTU units, which is the sign of an efficient dual hose design.

The maker claims it cools more than twice as fast and as strongly as a conventional unit, which is a marketing figure to treat with care. Even so, the SACC number gives it a real lead on paper. It is the most expensive unit in the guide, and the tradeoff against the Whynter is a newer design and a heating mode, against a more established product with a built in dehumidifier and auto drain.

A single hose in hose cable is thicker than a normal hose, so check the window kit fits your window and how it routes. Plan the exhaust route to be short, because long hoses lose capacity. Wash the filter every two weeks, and drain the unit at season end.
products.bestFor: Large rooms where the highest rated cooling and a heating mode justify the cost.
pros: A 12,000 BTU SACC rating is the highest stated cooling figure in this guide
Hose in hose design draws outside air instead of room air
Variable speed inverter keeps temperature steady and cuts noise
Heating mode adds use in spring and autumn
cons: Highest cost in the lineup and a large unit to move
Faster cooling claim is marketing and the thicker hose needs a compatible window kit

products.name: BLACK+DECKER Smart Portable AC with Heat, 14,000 BTU, 10,200 BTU SACC
products.description:
The BLACK+DECKER smart unit lists 14,000 BTU on the older ASHRAE basis and 10,200 BTU on the SACC basis, which is the number you should use to size a room. The listing claims coverage of up to 700 square feet, a heating mode as a four in one unit, and Wi-Fi with voice control. The body is 16.5 inches wide, 14.06 inches deep and 27.09 inches tall.

The SACC figure is about 73 percent of the headline number, which is typical, and it is lower than the Midea Duo at 12,000 despite the same 14,000 BTU label. It does not describe a dual hose design in our data, so assume a conventional single hose, which loses some efficiency as it pulls room air out through the vent. It costs less than the dual hose units, and it is the most affordable way to get a high capacity with a heat mode.

The 700 square foot claim is generous. Real coverage depends on ceiling height, sun and heat sources, so size by the SACC number and not the area. Plan the hose route, wash the filter every two weeks and keep clear space around the intake.
products.bestFor: Large rooms that need high capacity and heat mode at a lower cost than dual hose.
pros: 10,200 BTU SACC and a 700 sq ft claim suit a large living room
Heating mode adds use in winter and shoulder seasons
Wi-Fi and voice control allow remote scheduling
Lower cost than the dual hose Whynter and Midea Duo
cons: No dual hose design is described, so efficiency is lower than the dual hose units
The 700 sq ft coverage claim is generous for a sunny room

products.name: BLACK+DECKER 10,000 BTU Portable Air Conditioner, 6,300 BTU SACC, 450 sq ft

specList.label: Coverage
specList.value: Rooms up to 450 sq ft claim

products.description:
This BLACK+DECKER is the plain, mid size portable unit. It lists 10,000 BTU on the ASHRAE basis and 6,300 BTU on the SACC basis, a coverage of up to 450 square feet, and three modes: cooling, dehumidifying and fan. The Follow Me remote reads the temperature at the remote rather than at the unit, so the room around you is the one that cools. The body is 15.3 inches wide, 14 inches deep and 24.8 inches tall.

The SACC number is the honest one. It is about 63 percent of the headline figure, and it says this is a unit for a room of perhaps 200 to 300 square feet, not 450. It costs less than the 14,000 BTU models, and it does not describe a dual hose design, so expect a single hose. For a medium sized bedroom or a small living room, it is a reasonable choice at a moderate price.

Keep the exhaust hose short and straight, and seal the window kit well. The unit drains into a tank or a hose, so check how it handles humidity in your room. Wash the filter every two weeks, and let the unit dry before storing it for the winter.
products.bestFor: Medium bedrooms and small living rooms that need a sensible capacity at a moderate cost.
pros: 6,300 BTU SACC is a realistic rating for a medium room
Follow Me remote cools around the person holding it
Three modes cover cooling, dehumidifying and fan use
Lower cost than the 14,000 BTU models in the lineup
cons: The 450 sq ft claim is optimistic against a 6,300 BTU SACC rating
No dual hose design is described, so it loses some efficiency

products.name: DREO Portable Air Conditioner 318S, 8,000 BTU ASHRAE, 5,000 BTU DOE, Smart

specList.label: Coverage
specList.value: Cools up to 14 ft away, stated

products.description:
The DREO 318S is a compact smart unit for bedrooms. It lists 8,000 BTU on the ASHRAE basis and 5,000 BTU DOE, which is the same as SACC, with cool, fan and dry modes and a patented self evaporating system that the listing calls drainage free. The IceCool system claims to increase coverage up to 14 feet from the unit.

Drainage free operation is the selling point. Most portable units collect water that you must empty or drain, while a self evaporating design sends the moisture out with the exhaust. It works best in moderate humidity, and in a damp room the system can still fill a tank, so keep a drain route in mind. It costs more than the HOMCOM 8,000 BTU and about the same as the BLACK+DECKER 10,000 BTU, and it is quieter and smarter than either.

The 14 foot claim is a best case, and the real effect depends on the room. Set it in the centre of the cooling zone, with the intake clear of curtains. Wash the filter every two weeks, and check the app for updates.
products.bestFor: Bedrooms and small rooms where emptying a water tank is a chore.
pros: Self evaporating design aims to avoid emptying a drain tank
Lists both ASHRAE and DOE numbers, so sizing is honest
Smart control and cool, fan and dry modes cover most needs
Compact body fits a small bedroom or office
cons: 5,000 BTU DOE suits only a small room, not a large living room
Drainage free operation can still need a drain route in humid weather

products.name: Midea 8,500 BTU ASHRAE Portable Air Conditioner, 5,000 BTU SACC, App Control

specList.label: Coverage
specList.value: Stated to cool up to 150 sq ft

specList.label: Control
specList.value: SmartHome app for iOS and Android

products.description:
The Midea 8,500 is a small unit with an honest coverage claim. The listing states 8,500 BTU ASHRAE, 5,000 BTU SACC and cooling for up to 150 square feet, with app control through the SmartHome app and an easy to read digital display. Many 8,000 BTU units claim much larger areas, which makes this a more cautious and more believable specification.

The 150 square foot figure is the most useful detail in the guide, because it matches what 5,000 BTU of SACC can really do in a standard room. It costs a little more than the HOMCOM and less than the DREO. The compromise is capacity: it is a bedroom or a study cooler, not a living room unit, and in a big space it will run all the time and still fail to cool.

Expect a single hose design that is not described as dual. Plan the hose and the window kit, keep the filter clean and check the drain. The app is helpful for scheduling the unit before you get home.
products.bestFor: Small bedrooms and offices where an honest, compact unit is enough.
pros: Honest 150 sq ft coverage claim matches its 5,000 BTU SACC rating
SmartHome app allows scheduling from a phone
Lists both ASHRAE and SACC capacity for easy sizing
Low to mid cost for a compact app controlled unit
cons: Only suits a small room, and will struggle in a sunny living room
Single hose design loses some efficiency compared with dual hose models

products.name: HOMCOM 8,000 BTU Portable Air Conditioner, 4 in 1, Rooms to 344 sq ft

specList.label: Coverage
specList.value: Rooms up to 344 sq ft claim

products.description:
The HOMCOM is the cheapest portable unit here. It lists 8,000 BTU, a coverage claim of 344 square feet, four modes (cool, dehumidify, ventilate and sleep), a 24 hour timer with auto cut off and four swivel casters. The sleep mode only works with the remote, according to the listing, which is a small detail worth knowing.

The 8,000 BTU figure is not stated on the SACC basis, so the real cooling is probably lower. A rating of 8,000 BTU ASHRAE corresponds to perhaps 5,000 SACC, which is a bedroom unit, not a 344 square foot cooler. It costs less than every other model here, so for a small, sealed room it is the practical entry point. It does not describe a dual hose, so expect single hose losses.

Compact casters make it easy to move from room to room. Seal the window kit well, because gaps let hot air in. Check how it deals with water, since it has a tank or a drain hose. Clean the filter every two weeks.
products.bestFor: Small rooms and tight budgets that need a simple, mobile cooler.
pros: Lowest cost in the guide for a four mode portable unit
24 hour timer with auto cut off allows overnight scheduling
Four swivel casters make it easy to move between rooms
Compact body suits a small bedroom or office
cons: Capacity is stated in plain BTU and not SACC, so real cooling is lower
Sleep mode only works with the remote, and the unit is single hose

buyingCriteria.explanation: Portable units list an older ASHRAE or nominal BTU and, when you are lucky, the DOE SACC figure, which is the real cooling after losses. The BLACK+DECKER 14,000 BTU lists 10,200 SACC, the 10,000 BTU lists 6,300 SACC and the Midea 8,500 lists 5,000 SACC. SACC is often about 60 to 75 percent of the headline number.

A single hose unit pulls room air over its condenser and pushes it outside, creating a slight vacuum that draws warm air in through gaps. A dual hose unit like the Whynter and Midea Duo brings in outside air instead, so it does not waste cooled air. Dual hose models cost more and are bulkier, but they cool a room better at the same capacity.

Square footage is a starting point only. Ceiling height, sun exposure, kitchens, electronics and the number of people all add load. A sunny living room needs more capacity than a shaded bedroom of the same size. The HOMCOM claims 344 square feet and the BLACK+DECKER 10,000 BTU claims 450, but their SACC ratings suggest smaller rooms.

The compressor sits in the room, so every portable unit is audible. Inverter models like the Whynter, the Midea Duo and the DREO vary speed and cycle less, which usually sounds calmer than an on off compressor. Maker decibel figures are not measured the same way, so compare owner descriptions rather than the number.

Cooling removes moisture from the air, and the unit must get rid of it. Some collect it in a tank that you empty, some drain through a hose and some evaporate it into the exhaust. The Whynter has an auto drain and the DREO is self evaporating. In humid rooms, even self evaporating units may need a drain hose.

Every unit needs a window kit and a short, straight hose to the outdoors. A long or kinked hose loses capacity and radiates heat back into the room. Gaps around the kit let warm air in, so seal them with the supplied foam or tape. Check your window type, because sliding, sash and casement windows need different kits.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity and ratings
howWeEvaluated.description: We evaluated each unit by SACC where stated and by ASHRAE otherwise, from the 5,000 SACC Midea 8,500 to the 12,000 SACC Midea Duo. We treated coverage claims as best case.

howWeEvaluated.title: Hose design
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated the dual hose Whynter and Midea Duo from units that describe no dual design. We noted the efficiency gap.

howWeEvaluated.title: Noise and compressor
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted inverter compressors and their steadier running. We treated maker noise figures as unreliable.

howWeEvaluated.title: Water and upkeep
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared auto drain, self evaporating and tank designs. We considered the filter wash and end of season steps.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at patterns in owner feedback on noise, window kit fit and cooling in hot weather. We did not copy ratings or counts.

cards.label: Dual hose
cards.text: The Whynter and Midea Duo draw outside air and so waste less cooled air. They cost more, weigh more and cool a large room better.

cards.label: Single hose
cards.text: The BLACK+DECKER, DREO, Midea 8,500 and HOMCOM units cost less and are lighter. They pull room air through, so they lose some efficiency.

howToChoose.note: Choose dual hose for large, sunny rooms and single hose for small bedrooms.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A SACC rating suited to the room, a dual hose design if it is large or sunny, an inverter compressor and a clear route for the hose. Place it away from the sofa to manage noise.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Whynter and Midea Duo suit a large living room, the BLACK+DECKER 14,000 gives high capacity at a lower cost, and the smaller units suit bedrooms.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: The room is large, sunny or used all day, or you need quieter running. Dual hose inverter units cost more and run better.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: The room is small and you only need cooling at night. The HOMCOM and Midea 8,500 cost the least and do the job.

maintenance.why: A clogged filter cuts airflow and cooling.
A full tank stops the unit.

maintenance.task: Check the hose and window kit seal
maintenance.why: Gaps let warm air back in and waste capacity.
Dust reduces efficiency and raises noise.
Drain all water and run fan mode until dry.

faq.q: What is the difference between ASHRAE and SACC?
faq.a: ASHRAE is an older, higher figure from ideal conditions, and SACC is the DOE rating that includes real world losses. Size by SACC, as in the 10,200 SACC on the BLACK+DECKER 14,000.

faq.q: Is a dual hose unit worth the cost?
faq.a: For a large or sunny room, yes, because it does not pull cooled air outside. For a small bedroom, a single hose unit is enough.

faq.q: Can a portable air conditioner replace a window unit?
faq.a: It can cool a room, but it costs more to run and is louder. If a window unit fits your window, it is usually the better choice.

faq.q: Do I need to empty the water?
faq.a: It depends on the model. The Whynter has an auto drain and the DREO self evaporates, while the HOMCOM may need a tank or hose.

faq.q: How big a room can a 14,000 BTU unit cool?
faq.a: Makers claim 700 square feet, but the SACC figure of 10,200 to 12,000 suggests a moderate to large room. Sun and ceiling height reduce it.

faq.q: Why is my unit so loud?
faq.a: The compressor sits inside the room, so noise is unavoidable. Inverter models are calmer, and a longer distance from the sofa helps.
